Sonova (SOON-CH): an excellent business whose share price has caught up with the investment case, with the two 2027 results as the next test

Written 27 November 2026. Share price CHF 291.80 (22 November 2026); market value about CHF 17bn. Fiscal years end on 31 March (FY2027 is the year to 31 March 2027). Definitions and model notes are in the end-notes.

#0 Summary: key insights, implications and conclusions

Sonova's business is excellent and its investment case is good, but the share price has caught up with both, and the next two reporting periods will test the case on the measures the market watches. Sonova is the largest maker in a five-player hearing-aid oligopoly that competes on two-year product cycles rather than on price. The company earns a 75% gross margin and a 20% to 21% return on capital employed, and it has gained wholesale market share for eleven consecutive quarters. A completely new leadership team has, within fourteen months, exited the failed consumer business, reorganised the company into regions, launched a CHF 90m savings programme, and beaten expectations and raised guidance at both of its results. FY2027 is close to secured: the first half is reported, Sonova has already earned the 22.3% core EBIT margin that the full year needs over the last twelve months, and the raised guidance requires only 1% to 6% core EBIT growth in the second half.

Five conclusions matter most for the investment decision.

  1. The FY2027 earnings step-up is real, but it mostly reflects the removal of headwinds, and the share price already reflects it. Core EPS was flat in Swiss francs for four years (CHF 11.14, 10.06, 10.43, 10.42) while local-currency earnings compounded at 10% to 16% a year. Two headwinds explain the gap: the strong franc, which cost about 5 points of EBIT growth a year, and a tax rate that rose from 8% to 16%. In FY2027 the franc is neutral for the first time in four years, the tax increase is complete and the costs of ramping up the Mexicali plant are gone, so core EPS rises about 14% to about CHF 11.8. Consensus (CHF 11.80) already carries that figure. The shares re-rated from 14.6x two-year-forward earnings (CHF 167 in April 2026) to 21.3x (CHF 292), so about two-thirds of the 47% twelve-month share-price rise came from the higher multiple.
  2. The next two half-year results will show core EPS growth of about (1)% and +2%, after +36%, even though core EBIT grows 6% to 7% in each half. Nearly 30% of the first half's EPS growth came from a financial result of CHF (1.7)m (against CHF (31)m a year earlier), which will not repeat. Five further drags all land in the half to September 2027, which Sonova reports in November 2027: the second-half investment step-up, the end of tax safe-harbour relief on 31 March 2027, the annualisation of the Costco and Virto R gains, the hardest wholesale comparison of the cycle (+11%) and Amplifon's phase-out of Sonova products. No broker note I have seen combines these items.
  3. The Swiss franc is the only open forecast requirement that Sonova does not control, and the risk around the franc is one-sided. The Viewforth base case assumes the franc reduces sales growth by 1 point a year (1.6 points of core EBIT growth) from FY2028. Over sixteen years the franc drag averaged 2.5 to 3 points, and the franc was neutral or better in only about one year in three. Consensus assumes no drag at all. Each extra point of franc strength removes about 1.6% of EPS, and the franc explains about 40% of the difference between the forecast and the last four years.
  4. The balance sheet is the one favourable item the market knows about but has not priced. Net debt falls to about 0.75x EBITDA by March 2027, below management's 1.0x to 1.5x corridor, and to about 0.5x by March 2028. Sonova therefore has CHF 0.3bn to 0.5bn of spare capacity now and CHF 0.6bn to 0.9bn in a year, which no estimate includes (consensus holds debt flat). Management prefers acquisitions to buybacks; a CHF 0.7bn to 1.0bn retail acquisition adds 5% to 7% to EPS but costs 60 to 80 basis points of group margin and about 3 points of return on capital employed. The paradox of the case is that the likeliest source of upgrades is also the event that most tests the new team's capital discipline.
  5. The risk/reward skew is neutral now and turns negative from May to November 2027, before turning positive again. For six months the reported numbers are low-risk and carry little new information. From May to November 2027 the range of outcomes widens and leans down: the Viewforth FY2028 core EPS forecast is CHF 12.5, with four chances in five of landing between CHF 11.6 and CHF 13.2, while consensus (CHF 12.84) sits in the upper third of that range and has about a one-in-three chance of being reached. Over the last six months the sector has rewarded upgrades rather than low valuations, and operating upgrades are unlikely before November 2027. Beyond November 2027, balance-sheet deployment, the savings programme reaching full rate and the next product platform (about August 2028) rebuild the positive skew. The attractive entry point existed in May 2026 at 16x; the next one is more likely to come from a reset toward 17x to 19x (CHF 220 to 240) around the two 2027 results than from a continued rise from today's price.
Where I differ from the market. The sell-side is right in its words and wrong in its numbers. The brokers' mean rating is Hold and their mean target (CHF 283) is below the share price, but their forecasts assume a neutral franc, 7.3% revenue growth in francs in FY2028 and no balance-sheet deployment. The share price disagrees with the brokers because the marginal buyer is following price momentum (relative strength at the 94th percentile) and the catch-up of stale estimates. I agree with the Hold-rated brokers on the next twelve months. I am more constructive than they are on 2028 to 2029, when the balance sheet and the two-year platform cycle give the case a second leg that they do not model.

The return from today's price is modest over 18 months and good over three years. At my fair multiple of about 21.5x two-year-forward earnings, the return is roughly +5% to +9% over 18 months and about +20% over three years. At Viewforth's guideline fair multiple of 23.81x, which I treat as the bull case, the model's return is +18.3% to 31 March 2028 and +33.0% to 30 September 2029. The guideline multiple becomes reachable on a deployment event or visible share gains for the EON platform among independent clinics.

#1 Tailwinds in the operating environment, and the absence of headwinds

Conclusion: the environment is favourable now and already priced, but the single external variable that decides reported earnings, the Swiss franc, is more likely to turn against Sonova than for it after March 2027.

The hearing-aid market has recovered from its 2023 to early-2025 trough, and every element of the recovery is already in the FY2027 numbers. Unit volumes grew about 4% in the first half of calendar 2026 and about 6% in the third quarter, and Sonova raised its FY2027 market assumption to 3% to 5% value growth from 2% to 4%. Input costs eased, the franc is guided neutral for FY2027, and over-the-counter (OTC) hearing aids have not become a threat four years after the US rule that allowed them. On-device artificial-intelligence processing raises the cost of competing and favours the two largest research-and-development spenders, Sonova and Demant.

Demand has a highly visible structural floor and a cyclical layer above it that should not be extrapolated beyond twelve months. The structural floor is about 4% volume growth a year, driven by ageing populations and low adoption (38% in developed channels, 4% in China and India). The cyclical layer is a replacement wave, pulled forward by four simultaneous premium launches in August 2026 and by France's four-year reimbursement renewal cycle. That cyclical premium annualises in the second half of calendar 2027.

The headwinds are arriving sooner than the tailwinds will last. Demant is the strongest competitor in a decade, and its Zeal custom device cut Sonova's share of custom devices bought by the US Department of Veterans Affairs (VA) from 61% to 43% to 45% within a quarter. Amplifon's purchase of GN Hearing, closing around the turn of the year, turns the largest hearing-aid retailer into a manufacturer. Payers are pressing on prices in reimbursed channels, a US trade investigation could end the industry's duty-free status, and banks expect the franc to strengthen.

So-what. The external picture for the next six to twelve months is the best Sonova has had in three years. Over eighteen to thirty-six months the picture is balanced: the market spike annualises, the franc most likely resumes a 2-to-3-point drag on EBIT growth, and the channel realignment around Amplifon-GN and Demant-KIND costs about half a point of wholesale growth a year. Independent clinics' resentment of GN's new owner may partly offset that loss, but I cannot size the offset.

Counter-case. At its Capital Markets Day on 24 November 2026, Demant cut its mid-term organic growth target to 5% to 7% and kept a market growth view of 4% to 6% with flat prices. If the market holds 5% to 6% growth through 2027 rather than fading to 4%, Sonova's FY2028 local-currency growth runs nearer 7% than my 6.3%.
Where I differ from the market. Consensus implicitly assumes the tailwinds persist (zero franc drag and market growth near 5%) and the headwinds arrive slowly (Amplifon's phase-out spread evenly). I assume the opposite ordering: the headwinds are nearer than the tailwinds are durable.
The franc is the one variable that decides reported earnings, and its risk is one-sided.

Score: 59, set by the Rater. A structural demographic floor (about 4% volume a year, low adoption) and a recovered market (value 3-5%, best in three years, input deflation, OTC a non-threat) are real positives, but the cyclical spike annualises within twelve months while the base-case franc drag returns from FY2028, Demant is the strongest rival in a decade and Amplifon-GN removes CHF 50-60m of revenue; over two to three years that nets to a mild positive, a touch above the 57 group score because the ageing floor is unusually durable.

#2 Internally driven corporate change forces, and the absence of problems

Conclusion: Sonova's internal change is real, fast, broad and self-funded, but its financial outputs mostly arrive in FY2029 to FY2031, and the one near-term decision the new team has not yet taken, how to deploy the balance sheet, is where its capital discipline will first be tested.

In fourteen months Sonova replaced its whole leadership and took six structural decisions. The new chair is Gilbert Achermann (formerly of Straumann). The new chief executive, from September 2025, is Eric Bernard, formerly chief executive of WS Audiology and 25 years at Essilor. The new finance chief is Elodie Carr-Cingari (formerly of Landis+Gyr), the new operations chief is Roberto di Fiore (formerly of WS Audiology), the research chief is also new, and three board seats were refreshed. Insiders are buying: the chair's holding rose 130%, every director bought or held shares, and the board raised shareholding requirements to 300% and 200% of fees.

The early results of the change programme are good, but most of the first-half gain came from the previous team's product cycle. The programme is among the broadest self-funded corporate change programmes in European medtech in 2025 to 2026. In the first half, core gross margin rose 230 basis points, core EBIT grew 22.9% in constant currency and free cash flow reached CHF 266m against CHF 60m. Most of that improvement, however, came from products launched under the previous team (Infinio in August 2024, Virto R, the Costco re-entry and VA share gains) and from the non-repeat of plant ramp-up costs. The new team's own outputs (net savings from FY2028, regional synergies, growth in Asia and the move of costs out of Switzerland) are still ahead.

Five problems remain.

  1. "One-off" costs recur every year: CHF 44m in FY2025, about CHF 87m of adjustments in FY2026 and CHF 35m to 40m guided for FY2027, so about CHF 0.50 a share sits permanently outside core EPS.
  2. Reinvestment absorbs part of the margin gain: the second half carries a reinvestment step-up in the low double-digit CHF millions, described as recurring, and the mid-term margin bridge reserves 1 to 3 points of margin for reinvestment against a 3-to-5-point gross gain.
  3. Executive incentives weaken just as acquisitions rise: from FY2027 the long-term incentive moves from options linked to return on capital to units linked to relative total shareholder return, while retail acquisitions increase and Sonova discloses no return hurdle or post-deal review (Amplifon applies a hurdle above 12%).
  4. Product reliability has slipped: reliability fell 6.6% in FY2026, and private practices describe repair delays and a "nickel-and-dime" support culture.
  5. The leadership team is new together: the finance, operations and research chiefs changed within months of each other during a restructuring.

So-what. The change programme supports roughly 35 to 40 basis points a year of local-currency margin expansion from FY2028, which is the middle of management's own algorithm, not the top. The expansion comes from volume leverage, about half of the CHF 90m of savings reaching EBIT, the implant business's recovery, lower reinvestment and retail mix.

Local-currency margin expansion a year from FY2028
Viewforth base (about half of CHF 90m to EBIT)35-40 bp
Counter-case (more than half to EBIT)50-70 bp
Sonova's CHF 6bn revenue ambition for FY2031 needs about CHF 1.1bn of acquired revenue on Viewforth's numbers and is not in the base case.
Counter-case. Peers have delivered savings programmes of this type on time or early: Demant raised its 2026 savings to DKK 300m from DKK 250m, GN's One-GN programme beat plan and Amplifon's Fit4Growth programme under-spent. Sonova itself delivered CHF 40m from its previous programme. If management lets more than half of the CHF 90m fall to EBIT, margin expands by 50 to 70 basis points a year, not 35.
Where I differ from the market. Brokers credit the change programme and the consumer exit as forward margin tailwinds. The consumer exit, however, is already in the restated comparative base, and the previous programme's savings were absorbed by marketing inflation. I give full credit to the execution of the announced steps and none to value creation from large acquisitions.

Score: 72, set by the Rater. A complete, self-funded reset in fourteen months (chair, CEO, CFO, COO, R&D chief, regionalisation, the loss-making consumer unit exited, CHF 90m savings programme, franc cost relocation, insider buying) with two beat-and-raise prints, but the first half's gains came mostly from the old team's product cycle, the new team's own outputs land in FY2029-31 and recurring one-offs, reliability slippage and untested capital allocation net against it; coherent with the 72 group score.

#3 Industry structure, business model, financial profile and management

Conclusion: Sonova combines a top-decile industry structure, a strong layered moat whose technological edge must be re-won every two years, an above-average financial profile and a much better management team; capital allocation is the one foundation not yet demonstrated.

The hearing-aid industry structure is among the strongest in medtech. Five makers hold 85% to 94% of a USD 7.7bn wholesale market, and they compete through two-year platform launches rather than on price. Wholesale list prices held through the soft market of 2023 to 2025, manufacturers passed through price rises of more than 10% for tariffs in 2025, and Demant chose in 2024 to lose a managed-care channel rather than discount. The barriers to entry are decade-long chip and software cycles, EU Medical Device Regulation and US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) class II approvals, audiologists' training on and familiarity with each maker's fitting software, and global service networks. No new maker has appeared, and OTC devices have taken about 1% of US units.

Retail is fragmented, which gives Sonova a long runway for bolt-on acquisitions. The USD 23bn retail market is split between independent clinics (40% to 50%), Amplifon (11% to 13%) and Sonova and Demant (about 7% each).

The industry has two fragilities: the downstream channel and the technology lead. The channel is consolidating (Amplifon-GN, Demant-KIND, Costco at more than 15% of US distribution, optical chains), and the technology lead rotates every two years.

Sonova's moat is layered: a durable base and a technological edge that rotates.

Durable layers
  • Switching costs in fitting software and clinic workflow
  • VA position: 53.5% of value, five-year fixed-price contracts
  • The Roger wireless-microphone ecosystem in schools
  • Custom moulds and five-to-six-year replacement cycles
  • Owned retail: about 3,600 clinics, 39% of revenue, about 15% of Sonova's wholesale volume
  • Lowest production cost in the industry: about 13.5% of sales against Demant's about 22%
Rotating layer
  • Proprietary silicon: DEEPSONIC, now Hypersonic in the EON platform, the only new-chip platform of the August 2026 launch wave
  • Industry experts cite a two-to-three-year lead in custom silicon; Bernstein says leads are matched within one to two cycles

The VA is the best natural experiment, and it shows Sonova is not inferior overall but beaten in one category. In the VA, prices are fixed and clinicians choose freely. Sonova's total value share rose 470 basis points to 53.5% in the year to September 2026, after Demant launched Zeal, while Sonova's custom-device share fell from 61% to 43% to 45%.

Sonova's financial profile is above average. Core gross margin is 74.7%, and the core EBIT margin is heading to 22.3% in FY2027 (wholesale above 30%, retail in the mid-teens, implants 6.8% against 11% to 14% historically). Return on capital employed is 20.9%, and Bernstein's peer comparison of return on invested capital puts Sonova at 19%, Demant at 12.7% and Amplifon at 9%. Net debt is 1.1x EBITDA including leases, interest cover is about 40x, and free cash flow after leases of about CHF 600m rises to CHF 800m (86% to 91% of core net income). The profile has four weaknesses: the permanent gap between core and reported earnings, a tax rate that rose from 8% to 16% and may drift to 18%, four years of flat EPS in francs, and a large reinvestment outlet (retail) that earns less than the core wholesale business.

Management is a clear improvement, but its capital allocation is unproven. The chief executive has acted fast and comprehensively. His record at Essilor is strong; his record at WS Audiology is one of slow integration under active owners, although the gross-margin fall sometimes cited against him predates his tenure. The strategy has the right priorities (innovation to raise adoption, local execution, operational excellence) and is bolder than its predecessor in organisation and Asia. It is conventional, however, in its two biggest bets (premium platforms and the retail roll-up) and late in custom devices, where an instant-fit device is promised "within 18 months". Management communicates specifically on the growth algorithm and opaquely on customer and channel economics. The company's five-year delivery record is mixed (an August 2022 profit warning, deliveries at the low end of ranges and a withdrawn mid-term framework); the new team's record is two beats.

Where I differ from the market. The market pays Sonova a 23% premium to Demant (21.3x against 17.6x) for lower earnings volatility (a standard deviation of organic growth of 3.0 against 4.5). The historical premium was 10% to 15%, and Demant currently has the stronger product momentum and the larger upgrades. The quality gap is real, but the premium is at the wide end of its range.

Score: 78, set by the Rater. A top-decile five-maker oligopoly competing on platforms not price, number one with layered switching-cost, VA and owned-retail moats and the industry's lowest production cost, backed by a 90th-percentile gross margin, ROIC at the 78th percentile (peer-leading 19-21% on the memo's basis) and the steadiest organic growth in the peer group; held below Reply because the technology edge must be re-won every two years, retail reinvestment earns less than the core and management's capital allocation is unproven, which is why it sits a little above the 60-76 groups' blend.

#4 Conservative guidance, sell-side expectation management, and the track record

Conclusion: Sonova's guidance is conservative in the company's favour and the new team has beaten twice, but the November raise only brought guidance level with consensus, so the next guidance event (18 May 2027) is more likely to be read as "FY2028 guided below the Street" than as another beat.

The raised FY2027 guidance needs only a modest second half, and the Viewforth base sits at the top of the range. Sonova set FY2027 guidance in May 2026 below where second-half FY2026 run-rates pointed: sales +5% to 8%, core EBIT +7% to 10%, market growth 2% to 4% and a franc drag of 2 to 3 points. In November the company raised guidance to sales growth of 6% to 8% in local currencies and core EBIT growth of 10% to 13% in constant currency (CHF 839m to 862m on the restated base of CHF 762.9m), with the franc neutral. Because first-half core EBIT grew 22.9%, the second half needs only +1% to +6% core EBIT growth and about +5% wholesale growth, against +11% in the first half. The Viewforth base is core EBIT of about CHF 864m, at the top of the range, with second-half wholesale growth of 8% (Costco incremental for five of the six months, and the premium Sphere model about two-thirds of EON units). The chance that FY2027 core EBIT exceeds the top of the range is about even.

Management's informal tone is more confident than its formal numbers. Management describes EON conversion as "considerably faster than baseline", says it has "ample firing power" and adds "don't expect our ambition to go down". The chief executive declines to discuss Costco, large customers or channel margins.

The track record splits in two: misses and withdrawals under the old team, two beats under the new one. The new team beat in May 2026 (a second-half margin of 25.4% against 24.1% expected) and in November 2026 (core EBIT 10% and core EPS 19% above consensus). Before that, the company missed profit guidance in two of six years (FY2023 and FY2024), issued a profit warning in 2022, lost the Costco contract, withdrew its mid-term guidance in late 2025 and cut its floor in March 2026. Sell-side FY2028 EPS forecasts have risen 9% in six months and 5% in twelve.

Sonova's guidance is conservative against the company's own likely outcome, but no longer conservative against market expectations. The new team's pattern is to guide low, raise once on first-half evidence and leave room, which is the early stage of a deliberate sandbagging approach. The November raise, however, only took guidance to where analysts already were (Deutsche Bank: "consensus already there"). Consensus revenue (CHF 3,885m) sits at the top of the sales range and consensus EBIT (CHF 868m) at the top of the profit range.

The May 2027 results should land "as expected" on FY2027, but the first FY2028 guidance will most likely sit below consensus. I expect the first FY2028 guidance to repeat the shape of May 2026: sales growth of 5% to 7% in local currencies, core EBIT growth of 7% to 10% in constant currency, and the franc at early-May spot rates. If the franc follows the banks' forecast paths, the guidance will state a 1-to-2-point drag on sales and a 2-to-3-point drag on EBIT and will sit wholly below consensus.

#5 Pricing power, operating leverage, financial leverage, cost-out and feedback loops

Conclusion: Sonova has strong operating leverage and a credible cost programme, but management's reinvestment band and the franc mean that about 6% local-currency growth converts into about 8% to 9% core EBIT growth and 6% to 8% core EPS growth in francs: good rather than outsized.

Operating leverage is material in local currency but has been invisible in francs for six years. With a 75% gross margin and fixed or semi-fixed costs of 45% to 50% of sales (research and development about 6%, retail clinic costs 25% to 28%, wholesale selling and administration about 15%), each point of local-currency sales growth moves core EBIT by about 1.6% to 1.9%. The incremental margin is 35% to 40% on volume and close to 100% on price. Over FY2021 to FY2026, however, the FactSet adjusted EBIT margin moved only between 19% and 23%, because currency translation absorbed the leverage and management recycled part of it into reinvestment.

The first half's 59% incremental margin overstates the lasting leverage. CHF 10m to 15m of non-repeating plant ramp-up costs flattered the first half, so only about two-thirds of the 250-basis-point margin gain is lasting.

Sonova also has a proven cost lever on the downside. In FY2021 sales fell 7% in local currency while the margin rose 200 basis points, which shows management can cut CHF 50m to 100m of costs when demand falls.

Pricing power is real and used moderately; it defends the margin rather than drives it. The evidence of pricing power is strong. Sphere carries a 10% price premium over Infinio in the VA, the 2025 VA contract reset gave Sonova a weighted 26% price rise fixed for five years, list prices held through the downturn, and Phonak (Sonova's main brand) is the least promotional maker and refuses to negotiate prices with independent clinics. Channel mix, however, caps the group's average selling price (Costco at USD 300 to 400 a device, managed care, the VA at USD 540), and Demant priced Zeal 42% above its standard device where Sonova chose a 10% premium and volume. About one point a year of price and mix (CHF 40m to 45m) roughly offsets 2.5% to 3% inflation on a CHF 2.0bn operating-cost base.

Average selling price is a misleading indicator for Sonova, because Costco lowers it while earning a high-20s EBIT margin. Monitor wholesale gross margin and VA value share instead.

Financial leverage is nil. Net interest of about CHF 22m to 30m is 2% to 3% of core EBIT, so a 10% move in EBIT moves EPS by about 10.3%. The balance sheet matters only through its under-use (see #2 and #7).

The cost-out programme is credible on delivery, but only about half of the savings reaches EBIT, mostly after FY2028. Most of the net saving shows in gross margin, which rises from 75.1% in FY2027 toward 76% by FY2031. Moving costs out of Switzerland is a hedge more than a saving: shifting 5 points of costs out of the country cuts Sonova's transaction sensitivity to a franc move by about a third from FY2029.

Reinforcing feedback loops dominate through FY2028, and balancing loops dominate from FY2029.

Reinforcing loops, dominant through FY2028

  • Platform share: Marvel lifted VA share from 39% to 53% and held it; Infinio gave eleven quarters of share gains
  • Rising minimum efficient scale in AI silicon: GN sold its hearing business and Starkey is losing share
  • Cash building into deployable capacity

Balancing loops, dominant from FY2029

  • Technology leads revert within one to two cycles
  • Retail customer acquisition costs rise (USD 450 to 800 a client)
  • Channel conflict: Sonova is both a retailer and the supplier to independents, who take 43% of its wholesale
  • Management's deliberate reinvestment
  • Buyback efficiency halves between 16x and 21x earnings

So-what for the numbers. From FY2028, core EBIT grows about 1.3 to 1.4 times as fast as revenue in francs (a margin gain of 35 to 40 basis points a year), against about 1.0 times over FY2022 to FY2026. Richard's test, whether revenue growth produces outsized profit growth, is met in local currency and only partly met in francs.

Counter-case. If management holds the reinvestment step-up at the low end and the savings run ahead of plan, as peers' programmes did, core EBIT grows 1.6 to 1.8 times as fast as revenue for two years and the margin reaches 24% by FY2029 rather than FY2031.
Where I differ from the market. Consensus margins equal Viewforth's (22.3%, 22.7%, 23.0% and 23.4% for FY2027 to FY2030). The disagreement is not about operating leverage but about the revenue that the leverage is applied to, which depends on the franc and on growth.

Score: 63, set by the Rater. Structurally real gearing: a 75% gross margin with 45-50% of costs fixed gives 1.6-1.9x EBIT per point of local growth, held pricing (VA reset +26% fixed five years, list prices kept through the downturn), a credible CHF 90m cost-out and a platform-share loop; but financial leverage is nil, price mainly offsets inflation, management recycles part of the leverage into reinvestment and the franc absorbs it, so core EBIT grows only 1.3-1.4x revenue and EPS about 1.4x, below the median company's 2x; two gears, one strong, sits between the 50 and 75 levels.

#6 Forecast financials: scope for double-digit growth and for higher growth and margins than the past

Conclusion: the forecasts show the first sustained growth in franc EPS in five years (about 8% a year, and 14% in FY2027), built mostly on headwinds ending rather than on new strengths. FY2027 is secured, FY2028 consensus is fair to demanding, and FY2029 to FY2030 consensus needs a neutral franc or a deployed balance sheet.

The table shows the Financial Analyst's model (the forecasts of record) and the Analyst's corrected cross-check, which I use for judgement. The model's revenue and EPS are about 3% too low for a purely mechanical reason, explained in end-note 2.

Franc EPS growth returns to about 8% a year, but reaching double digits needs a neutral franc, balance-sheet deployment or a won next platform. In local currency, core EBIT grows about 13% in FY2027 and about 8% to 9% a year after that, and core EPS grows about 10% a year before the franc. In francs, core EPS compounds at about 8% a year from FY2026 to FY2031. Double-digit franc EPS growth needs one of three things: a neutral franc (adding about 1.6 points), deployment of the balance sheet (adding 1.5 to 3 points a year for a buyback, or 5 to 7 points once for an acquisition) or a won next platform.

About 6 of the 8 points of EPS growth come from headwinds ending. Measured against the last four years' zero EPS growth, about 3.5 points a year come from the franc drag shrinking, about 2 from the tax rate no longer rising, about 2 from margin expansion and about 0.8 from buybacks. Local-currency growth was there all along.

Growth does not break from the past, but margins do, and the margin destination is not unprecedented. Local-currency growth of about 6% equals the five-year organic record of 5% to 6% plus a point of bolt-on acquisitions. The core EBIT margin rises from 21.2% to 23.7%, roughly where Sonova stood in FY2022 on FactSet's basis (23.3%) while it still carried the loss-making consumer unit, and the forecast uses less than half of management's margin bridge. Free cash flow nearly doubles from FactSet's historical CHF 340m to 432m as payables and inventory normalise and EBITDA grows.

Consensus for FY2029 and FY2030 is, in effect, the Viewforth forecast with a neutral franc, a point a year more growth and none of the deployment that would be needed to achieve that growth. In FY2027 the cross-check is level with consensus on every line. In FY2028 it is 2.5% below on revenue, EBIT and EPS, all of it from revenue: one point from the franc and one point from local-currency growth, found in retail and implants rather than wholesale, with identical margins. In FY2029 to FY2030 it is 5% to 7% below on EBIT and EPS, made up of three points of cumulative franc drag and 2.4 points of growth.

Where I differ from the market. On FY2027, nowhere. On FY2028 to FY2030, I am below consensus on revenue and EPS and level on margin, and I think consensus is reachable only through an event that it does not model.

Score: 60, set by the Rater. 5-10% gives C; placed a little above mid-band because the growth is organic and the margin path rises from 21.2% to 23.7%, but it only returns to the FY2022 level and is built mostly on headwinds ending (franc, tax) rather than new strength, with later years below consensus.

#7 Scope for upgrades to guidance, sell-side estimates and the narrative over 6 to 12 months

Conclusion: the easy upgrade phase (May to November 2026, +9% to FY2028 EPS) has passed. Over the next six to twelve months, estimates are more likely to drift down by a few per cent than up, and the only large upgrade in prospect is an acquisition, which is also a risk.

No scheduled event can raise FY2027 guidance before 18 May 2027, and the guidance events after that are more likely to hold or disappoint than to raise. An intra-period guidance raise has about a one-in-ten chance; Sonova's last was in February 2020. In the six guided years before FY2027 the company raised mid-year once and cut once.

Sell-side estimates will keep rising for about three months for a mechanical reason that carries no information. Six of the FactSet estimates behind the FY2027 median are stale (for example RBC at CHF 10.16, Oddo at 10.45, Vontobel at 10.62 and Barclays at 10.74), and the consensus mean rises 4% to 5% as those brokers refresh their models.

After the refresh, I expect FY2028 consensus to drift down 1% to 3%, arriving at the two 2027 results rather than gradually. FY2028 consensus (CHF 12.84) is 2.7% above the Viewforth forecast. FY2029 consensus is more likely to be lower in a year (50%) than higher (30%). The segment most likely to miss in May is Cochlear Implants: consensus needs the implant business's second half to grow about 18%, although the Integro implant has launched only in Europe and has no FDA approval date. The miss would cost only CHF 5m to 8m of profit, but it would be the third in a row.

The largest and likeliest upgrade is an acquisition, and the acquisition is also the clearest test of the new team's capital discipline. Brokers add an acquisition's revenue and earnings on the day it is announced, but a retail deal lowers margin and return on capital and tests an unproven allocator, so the multiple gives back part of the upgrade. The downgrade risks are of similar size and centre on the franc and a US tariff.

The balance sheet is the one known, unpriced positive, and also the clearest test of capital discipline.

The market narrative will shift from "beat and raise" to "deceleration" by November 2027, and only new developments can broaden it again. Today's narrative is "beat and raise, EON momentum, consumer exit done, franc neutral, best-in-class margins". By November 2027 the words the market uses will be "deceleration", "tough comps", "franc", "reinvestment" and, if it happens, "acquisition". The narrative can broaden only on new developments: balance-sheet deployment, the instant-fit custom device (which DNB Carnegie expects in 2027), Integro approval in the US and the next platform (about August 2028). The known events (monthly VA data, completion of the Consumer Hearing sale and the FY2027 results) can only confirm the current narrative.

Where I differ from the market. The AlphaSense narrative report finds the favourable dynamics fully articulated, and the unfavourable ones articulated in words but absent from the numbers. No note discusses the cluster of small items that all take effect on 1 April 2027: the end of the tax safe harbour, the normalising financial result, the annualising reinvestment step-up, and the new IFRS 18 accounting standard moving currency gains and losses into operating profit. The market expects continued upgrades; I expect a flat-to-down drift in estimates from May 2027, and an upward one only on an event.

Score: 36, set by the Rater. Guidance, which counts most, cannot be raised before May 2027 and the first FY2028 guide is about three-in-four likely to sit below consensus, which already stands at the top of the raised FY2027 range; FY2028 consensus is 2.7% above the memo's forecast and expected to drift down 1-3% (about (0.3)x the 6% growth rate) after a short mechanical refresh, and the narrative is set to turn to deceleration and franc; only an acquisition (about 40% by May 2028) or buyback offers material upside, which keeps it a little below the 40 group score.

#8 Current momentum in guidance, estimates, narrative and share price, and the same for peers

Conclusion: share-price and guidance momentum are strong and estimate momentum is positive but spent, while ratings and targets have already turned. The pattern matches the end of prior hearing-aid upcycles, and Demant is the peer with stronger operating momentum on a lower multiple.

Guidance momentum is positive, with one raise. In November 2026 Sonova lifted its core EBIT growth range by three points and its sales growth floor by one point. In francs the swing was larger, from an implied +4% to 8% to +10% to 13%, because the expected franc drag of 2 to 3 points became neutral.

Sell-side momentum is positive on EPS, turning on EBITDA and negative on ratings. FY2028 consensus EPS rose 1% over one month, 6% over three and 9% over six. Consensus EBITDA fell 2% over one month, but only because brokers rebuilt their models on the continuing core basis with lower depreciation, so EBIT is the better measure. The mean target price rose 14% in a month and 35% in six, following the share price. The share of Buy ratings is 17%, down ten points in a month, and the mean rating is Hold. Rating changes run both ways: Jefferies moved up to Hold, Barclays is reported to have moved to Overweight and Morningstar rates the stock Underweight. The Viewforth dashboard pins sell-side momentum at C.

#9 Riskiness and simplicity of the forecasts and expectations

Conclusion: Sonova is a simple, trackable operating case, but its reported outcome is hostage to one external variable, the franc, and its share price carries 20% to 30% of downside to a fair trough multiple without any fundamental damage. That combination makes the case moderately risky rather than low-risk.

The case is simple: one segment drives the change in earnings, and the level of earnings is diffuse. Wholesale, which earns over 70% of core EBIT, drives the change in earnings. The level of earnings rests on a broad base: no customer above 5% of sales, 100 countries, 3,600 clinics and a 4% demographic growth floor. The chain from guidance to core EBIT is clear and built from stated blocks. The chain breaks in three places: between wholesale and retail profit (which Sonova does not disclose), between volume and price, and between core EBIT and EPS, where the financial result and tax moved EPS as much as operations did in the last two halves.

Practical rule: judge each Sonova result on constant-currency core EBIT and wholesale growth, not on core EPS.

The case is trackable for the franc and the VA, but blind elsewhere until 18 May 2027. Investors can track three things between results:

  • Monthly VA value share. The alarm level is below 50% for one month; the thesis breaks below 48% for two months, or if custom share falls below 40%. Always quote the basis, because unit share is already 50.9% against value share of 53.5%.
  • Daily exchange rates against Sonova's published sensitivities. A 5% move in EUR/CHF changes sales by CHF 70m and operating profit by CHF 25m; a 5% move in USD/CHF changes sales by CHF 65m and EBITDA by CHF 17m.
  • Peer reporting: Demant's quarterly results and Amplifon's post-deal Capital Markets Day.

Nothing reveals the second-half margin, the independent clinics (43% of wholesale and the highest prices) or retail economics before 18 May 2027. Sonova reports only twice a year, and its next result is also the first under the new IFRS 18 presentation standard, eighteen months after a change of headline metric.

The range of outcomes is narrow and symmetric to May 2027, then wider and skewed down for FY2028. For FY2027, the Viewforth core EPS forecast is CHF 11.8, with four chances in five of landing within ±2.5%. For FY2028 the forecast is CHF 12.5, with four chances in five of landing between CHF 11.6 and CHF 13.2 ((7.5)% to +5.5%), a left tail at about CHF 10.5 and a right tail at about CHF 13.9. Morgan Stanley's own bull, base and bear cases (CHF 13.89, 12.86 and 10.49) have the same shape. Half-year core profit has missed or beaten consensus by 5% to 10% at four of the last five results.

The downside items are correlated, which fattens the left tail. A risk-off episode lifts the franc and weakens private-pay demand at the same time, and a lost launch window and channel losses tend to arrive together.

The sudden share-price risks are mostly low-probability, but a return to a trough multiple alone would cost 20% to 30%.

Perception-driven risks can also move the shares without changing earnings. One weak month of VA data could move the stock 5% to 10%. Peer events, a rotation out of healthcare (where technology investors parked money in 2026), de-ratings of perceived "AI winners" and the franc acting as a barometer of European stress are the other triggers.

Hearing aids have low cyclicality in volume but high cyclicality in market share and sentiment, and the multiple reverts after every platform peak. US downturns in hearing-aid volume rarely last more than two quarters. Each of Sonova's last four platform peaks, however, was followed by a de-rating of several turns within six to eighteen months: from 31x at the Paradise peak to 15.6x after the August 2022 guidance cut, and from 25x at the Infinio peak to 14.6x in April 2026. Demant's More cycle ended with a 15% one-day share-price fall and 20% estimate cuts in six months. The precedent says Sonova's multiple reverts to the median unless management supplies an upgrade, a buyback or an integration.

Five judgements move the value of the shares most over one to two years. The arithmetic starts from the FY2028 base: revenue CHF 4,074m, core EBIT CHF 924m, core EPS CHF 12.5, a 17.5% tax rate and 59.3m shares. Each point of core EBIT is about CHF 9m, and each CHF 10m of EBIT is about CHF 0.14 of EPS.

  1. The franc after March 2027. The base case assumes a drag of 1 point on sales and 1.6 points on EBIT. If the drag equals the sixteen-year average (about 3 points on sales and about 5 on EBIT), revenue falls a further CHF 81m and EBIT CHF 30m (from 924 to 894, (3.3)%), and EPS falls from CHF 12.5 to 12.1. Compounded to FY2030, EPS is about CHF 13.4 instead of 14.4 (7)%. A 10% franc spike in a single quarter cuts EBIT by CHF 100m and EPS by 11% in that year. In the mirror case (EUR/CHF at 0.95 by end-2028, as Morgan Stanley forecasts), sales gain 2 points and EPS 3% to 4%.
  2. The launch window and wholesale share in FY2028. The base case assumes wholesale growth of 5.5% in local currency, including 1.5 points of share gain. If Sonova loses the launch window (no share gain and Amplifon's phase-out front-loaded), wholesale grows about 3.5%, revenue falls CHF 41m and, at a 50% incremental margin, EBIT falls CHF 20m. Adding a one-in-five chance of a rebate war in European independent clinics (50 to 100 basis points of wholesale gross margin, CHF 10m to 20m) takes the EBIT loss to CHF 30m to 40m ((3.5)% to (4.5)%) and EPS to about CHF 12.0. If Sonova wins the window (3.5 points of share gain), EBIT gains CHF 20m and EPS reaches about CHF 12.8.
  3. The margin: the reinvestment step-up, the savings and customer acquisition costs. The base case adds 40 basis points of margin, to 22.7%. A flat margin (the step-up annualising at CHF 30m, no net savings and rising retail customer acquisition costs) gives EBIT of CHF 908m (1.7)% and EPS of about CHF 12.3. A gain of 80 basis points (savings ahead of plan and the step-up at the low end) gives EBIT of CHF 940m (+1.7%) and EPS of about CHF 12.7. Each 40 basis points of margin is worth ±CHF 16m of EBIT and ±1.8% of EPS.
  4. Deployment of CHF 0.6bn to 0.9bn of balance-sheet capacity. A CHF 300m buyback at about CHF 320 a share retires 0.94m shares (1.6% of the count) and adds about 1.5% to EPS after interest forgone; consensus carries no buyback. A retail acquisition of CHF 0.7bn to 1.0bn at about 1.5x sales adds CHF 450m to 650m of revenue at a 14% margin, which is CHF 65m to 90m of EBIT. After CHF 15m to 20m of financing costs, pre-tax profit rises CHF 50m to 70m and EPS 5% to 7% from FY2029, while group margin falls 60 to 80 basis points and return on capital employed falls from about 21% toward 18%. No estimate includes either deployment.
  5. A US Section 232 duty. A 10% duty on about CHF 150m to 200m of landed US imports (from Vietnam and Switzerland) costs CHF 15m to 20m gross, or 2% of EPS. An unmitigated 25% duty costs CHF 40m to 50m, or 5% to 7% of EPS. With production shifted to Mexicali and prices passed through outside the VA (whose contracts allow no pass-through), the second-year effect falls to 1% to 2% of EPS.
Where I differ from the market. The sell-side's risk sections list the same items, but their models carry none of them. The market treats the case as simple and low-risk because FY2027 is simple and low-risk. I treat the case as simple in operations and moderately risky in reported francs, with the risk concentrated in one variable (the franc) and one reporting period (the half to September 2027).

Score: 61, set by the Rater. The operating case is simple, diffuse and low-leverage with low volume cyclicality, FY2027 near-known within 2.5% and an FY2028 cone of (7.5)% to +5.5% (four in five), but the reported outcome is hostage to a one-sided franc, the highest-margin channel is untrackable on semi-annual reporting, the downside items are correlated and sector precedent shows several-turn de-ratings after every platform peak, leaving 20-30% of share-price downside without fundamental damage; between the 48 and 58 groups and a little above for the clean balance sheet.

#10 Where the stock is in its lifecycle

Conclusion: the stock is late in its reinforcing phase, at peak delivery with the multiple ahead of earnings, and the November 2027 result is the dated test of whether it broadens on a new leg or stalls on the known ones.

The dashboard's rule places the stock in the "Broadening" phase, whose guideline multiple is 23.81x (the 80th percentile). My view is "Reinforcing, late", a notch further along, with the first test of "Stalling" due at the November 2027 result.

The thesis has deepened on one leg rather than added new ones, which marks a reinforcing phase rather than a broadening one. The leg that has deepened is the wholesale platform cycle: EON, VA share at a five-year high, Costco and Virto R. The candidate new legs (balance-sheet deployment, the instant-fit custom device, Integro in the US and net savings) are undated or arrive in FY2029. Delivery is at its peak: the margin step has been earned, the guidance has been raised and two consecutive beats have been reported. Upgrades (+9% in six months) are ending in substance, and what continues is mechanical catch-up. The multiple has moved ahead of earnings (two-thirds of the share-price rise), the premium to Demant is twice its historical width, and ratings have turned.

The stock is not stalling yet, because nothing in the next six months is likely to disappoint on the numbers. The operating engine has the lowest growth volatility in the peer group, EON is the only new-chip launch of the window and is converting faster than plan, and the balance sheet gives management a lever to pull. The peer basket explains only 39% of the daily variance in Sonova's share price, so the share price and multiple are company-driven and this analysis bears directly on the outcome.

#11 The fair multiple

Conclusion: the guideline multiple of 23.81x is a bull-case multiple for March 2028 that needs an event consensus does not carry; the fair multiple for the next twelve months is about 21.5x, roughly where the shares already trade.

Viewforth's guideline multiple is 12% above today's multiple. For the Broadening phase, Viewforth's rule sets 23.81x two-year-forward earnings, the 80th percentile of the stock's own ten-year range (10th percentile 16.9x, median 20.8x, 75th percentile 23.2x, 90th percentile 25.6x). The multiple today is 21.3x (25 November 2026).

My fair multiple is about 21.5x for the next twelve months, between the ten-year median and today's multiple, with the guideline as the bull case for March 2028. Three reasons support that view.

  1. A peak-delivery multiple needs continuing upgrades, and the next two results are more likely to bring a below-consensus guide and near-flat EPS growth. Every prior hearing-aid peak reverted toward the median within six to eighteen months unless management supplied an upgrade, a buyback or an integration (see #8 and #9).
  2. The 23% premium to Demant is twice its historical range, although Sonova has the smaller upgrades and the weaker near-term momentum. The sector sits at the 11th percentile of its range, so no sector floor supports a company-specific premium.
  3. The business is better than it was at the last de-rating, which rules out a median or bear multiple but does not yet justify the 80th percentile. The consumer exit, a higher margin, lower leverage and better management argue against the ten-year median (20.8x) as the base and against the 13x to 14x bear multiples that brokers carry. They do not justify the 80th percentile until the second leg (deployment or the next platform) is dated. The ten-year 10th percentile (16.9x) is the fair trough.

Where I differ from the market. Brokers' target multiples (Morgan Stanley uses 21x for Sonova and 21.5x for Demant) sit near mine, and the share price is already at or above them. My view is below the guideline rule and above the brokers' bear cases.

#12 Total shareholder return (DuPont split)

Conclusion: at the guideline multiple the return is +18% over 18 months and +33% over three years, about half from earnings and a third from re-rating. At a fair multiple nearer today's, the return is roughly +5% to +10% over 18 months and about +20% to +25% over three years, most of it earned after the November 2027 test.

At the guideline fair multiple, the model's calculation on the forecasts of record gives +18.3% over 18 months and +33.0% over three years.

Over 18 months, earnings supply about half of the return and the re-rating about a third. Two-year-forward EPS rises from about CHF 13.3 to about CHF 14.5 as the forecast window rolls from FY2028/29 to FY2029/30, and the multiple re-rates from the model's 22.6x to 23.81x; dividends supply the rest. Over three years the earnings component dominates (+21%), because the forward window rolls onto the model's FY2030/31 EPS of CHF 14.1 to 15.2, while the multiple component is unchanged by construction. The annualised return therefore falls from 13% to 10.5% as the one-off re-rating is spread over a longer period.

Three adjustments change how the model's return should be read.

  1. Dividends: the model pays two dividends inside the 18-month period, but a buyer today receives only one (CHF 5.20 in June 2027, +1.8%), so the 18-month return is about +16.4%. The three-year figure is correct.
  2. The mechanical EPS understatement: correcting the model's revenue base lifts every year's EPS by about 3% and lowers today's multiple to about 21.9x. The correction moves roughly 3 to 4 points of return from the multiple component to the earnings component and adds about 3 points in total (about +20% over 18 months and about +36% over three years).
  3. The multiple: at my fair multiple of 21.5x rather than the guideline, the return is much lower, as the table shows.

Little of the return is available before May 2027, the drawdown risk sits between May and November 2027, and the bulk of the three-year return comes from late 2027 onward. Before May 2027 the numbers are known and the multiple is full. From late 2027 the second leg (balance-sheet deployment, net savings and the August 2028 platform) rebuilds upgrades.

A lower entry price would transform the three-year return. From a reset to about CHF 220 to 240 (17x to 19x), the three-year return at the guideline multiple would be 55% to 70%, far better than the market's likely return from today's price.
Where I differ from the market. Brokers' targets (mean CHF 283) imply a negative twelve-month return at their own multiples. The model's return at the guideline is higher than the brokers' because the guideline multiple is higher than theirs. My own view sits between the two: a modest positive return over 18 months with a wide band, and a good one over three years.

Score: 42, set by the Rater. About +8% gives D and maps to about 45; I take the memo's own fair-multiple case over the model's +18% at the guideline because the memo calls 23.81x its bull case, and place it a few points lower for the fat, correlated lower tail ((25)% at the trough multiple on lower EPS) and a return earned mostly after the November 2027 test, with the three-year check only modestly supportive.

#13 Summary conclusion

Sonova is a high-quality business, but its share price now reflects that quality, and the investment case to prepare for is a reset toward 17x to 19x around the two 2027 results.

Sonova operates in a top-decile industry structure, is run by a much-improved team and is at the point of peak delivery in a product cycle it has won. The FY2027 numbers are nearly in hand, the margin step is already in the trailing twelve months, and its local-currency operations are among the steadiest in European medtech.

What has changed since May 2026 is the share price. The shares have re-rated from the 10th percentile of their valuation range to the 60th, consensus has caught up with guidance, and the sector's reward for upgrades is about to meet a period in which operating upgrades are unlikely.

Reported franc earnings from here rest on three things: a franc that stays neutral (which Sonova has enjoyed in only about one year in three), a launch window whose outcome in the highest-margin channel cannot be tracked, and a balance-sheet decision that is both the likeliest upgrade and the clearest test of capital discipline.

The fundamental skew over six to twelve months is balanced to slightly negative. Over two to three years the skew is modestly positive, and more clearly positive from a lower entry price. The next upcycle's drivers are the next platform and balance-sheet deployment. Owning the shares from today's price needs the May 2027 results to deliver either a deployment or a confident FY2028 guide.

Thesis's Change Forces' Strength: 63, set by the Rater. A strong, broad internal reset (72) and a mild external positive (59) are real, but they reach profits only as about 7-8% EPS growth a year, below the Universe median, with FY2027's +14% mostly headwinds ending and the new team's outputs back-end loaded, so clearly positive inputs lifting profits only to about median growth sit in the low 60s.

Foundations' Robustness: 80, set by the Rater. A top-decile, price-disciplined oligopoly with a layered moat, non-discretionary ageing demand, the steadiest organic growth in its peer group, a 75% gross margin and low leverage (topic 3 at 78) is a top-decile franchise whose one ordinary part is the delivery record (topic 4 at 57: misses before the new team, two beats since), which keeps it at 80 rather than in the high 80s.

Setups' Fit/Crispness: 66, set by the Rater. In substance the case fits a cause for concern clearing in a high-quality, low-cyclicality business (consumer exit, new team, franc neutral, margin restored) with a corporate-change step-up behind it, but the step-up is back-end loaded, the case straddles a demand-driven and a change-driven setup, and today's problems (Demant taking custom share, reliability slippage, untested capital allocation) blur it; the lost low multiple the memo cites is price and is not counted here, so I sit above its C.

Case Riskiness: 60, set by the Rater. Topic 9 at 61: a simple, trackable, unlevered operating case with a narrow near-term cone, but one uncontrollable, one-sided variable (the franc), correlated downside clustered in one reporting period and a multiple carried by momentum with 20-30% de-rating risk on sentiment alone, like Richard's Arteche 60 for retracement risk rather than a complex case.

End-notes

  1. Basis of the figures. All figures are for continuing operations. "Core EBIT" and "core EPS" are Sonova's own measures: they are stated after amortisation of acquired intangibles and before restructuring and litigation costs. The forecasts of record are the Financial Analyst's model (update 2). Where the model carries a known mechanical understatement, the memo says so and gives the Analyst's corrected cross-check beside it. "Viewforth" refers to the house forecasts and view.
  2. Why the forecast table has two rows for revenue and EPS. The model builds FY2027 as the reported first half plus a forecast second half. It applies second-half growth to FactSet's pre-restatement half-year revenue (about CHF 1,791m) rather than to the company's continuing-operations figure of CHF 1,887m. The model's FY2027 revenue is therefore CHF 104m (2.7%) too low, and every later year inherits the shortfall, which is worth about 3% of EPS. The third-set Analyst changed the period input to force the right figure, but the model's phasing rule moved the periods back to match the annual input, so the correction did not take effect. The shortfall is a model mechanic, not a judgement, and the Financial Analyst has been asked to correct the base. On the model's understated EPS, the multiple on 22 November 2026 computes as 22.6x, about half a turn above the true 21.3x.
  3. Other model mechanics. The model pays two dividends inside FY2027, so its March 2027 net debt is about one dividend too high and its 18-month return counts a dividend that falls after the horizon. The model also does not deduct non-core cash costs of CHF 20m to 38m a year. I use the cross-check rows for judgement and the model rows where the instructions require the forecasts of record.
  4. Model inputs left unchanged. I left every model input as it stands. The franc assumption (a 1-point drag) is the midpoint between consensus and history, and the asymmetry around it belongs in the risk analysis, not the base case. The buyback in the model is a proxy for a deployment that is more likely to be an acquisition, and over the horizon the two differ by only about 0.3% of FY2028 EPS. The second-half growth judgement (7.8%) is right, and the fix for the revenue base belongs in the model.

How to read this page

Every rating of this stock on one page: the Rater's 1-100 number, its letter and the Rater's own reason (at most three sentences, taken from the ratings file; nothing newly written). The number is the company's approximate standing in the Universe of about 1,300 listed European companies (90 = better than about 9 in 10; 50 = typical). A letter follows its item's rule: rank among the stocks scored (A the top 10%; B+ and B the next 15%; C+, C and C- the next 25%; D the next 25%; F the bottom 25%); or Richard's cut-offs on the measure for the four numerical topics (forecast financials, current momentum, the fair multiple, total shareholder return). On the change-forces items the number carries a sign (50 = neither positive nor negative) and the letter is the rank, so read the two together. "9th of 30 stocks scored" is the stock's place on that item. A dashed badge is provisional (fewer than 30 stocks scored).
